variants.title: Run the evidence loop
variants.context: Safety evaluation is a control loop, not one pre-release event: map credible harms, measure by slice, enforce the gate with thresholds agreed before results were seen, then learn from exposure by promoting confirmed failures into protected regressions.
variants.prompt: A team is standing up safety evaluation for a new assistant. Put the loop in order.

items.text: Measure by slice with benign, boundary, and adversarial cases, preserving denominators and severity.
Learn from exposure by joining reports to exact versions and promoting failures into regressions.
Map credible harms from product context, affected stakeholders, misuse analysis, and prior incidents.
Enforce the gate using thresholds agreed before anyone inspected the candidate result.

variants.hint: Which step decides what deserves evidence at all?
variants.explanation: Risk discovery scopes the tests, measurement produces sliced evidence, the gate acts on it, and exposure feeds the next cycle.

variants.title: Run the evidence loop
variants.context: Safety evaluation is a control loop, not one pre-release event: map credible harms, measure by slice, enforce the gate with thresholds agreed before results were seen, then learn from exposure by promoting confirmed failures into protected regressions.
variants.prompt: A crisis-language harm is added after a user complaint. Put the work in order for the next candidate.

items.text: Build single-turn and multi-turn cases for that path and record grader identity with every label.
Compare the sliced result against the threshold that was fixed before the run.
Name the harm, the affected population, and the response path the system must take.
Watch the same harm in production and convert each confirmed miss into a protected case.

variants.hint: The complaint is an input to scoping, not yet evidence.
variants.explanation: A new harm re-enters the loop at scoping so its cases, thresholds, and monitoring are defined before the gate reads them.

variants.title: Run the evidence loop
variants.context: Safety evaluation is a control loop, not one pre-release event: map credible harms, measure by slice, enforce the gate with thresholds agreed before results were seen, then learn from exposure by promoting confirmed failures into protected regressions.
variants.prompt: A retrieval corpus changes, so the whole claim must be re-established. Put the loop in order.

items.text: Monitor the changed path in production and feed confirmed failures back as regressions.
Recheck which harms the new corpus can reach, including harms the old corpus could not.
Apply the predetermined thresholds and record which blockers fired for which slice.
Rerun the sliced suite against the frozen candidate that now includes the new corpus.

variants.hint: A changed corpus is a changed system, so where does the loop restart?
variants.explanation: Any change to model, prompt, policy, corpus, or tools restarts the loop at harm mapping rather than at the gate.

variants.title: Turn an attack into evidence
variants.context: A red-team finding becomes durable evidence in four steps: state the threat hypothesis, run the controlled exercise, triage the evidence for reproducibility and severity, then store a protected regression mapped to the release gate.
variants.prompt: A red teamer suspects a document can redirect the assistant. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Confirm reproducibility, severity, affected slices, exact versions, and immediate containment.
Store a minimized fixture with its expected boundary, owner, and release-gate mapping.
Name the actor, goal, access, system surface, target harm, and the control expected to hold.
Run the controlled exercise with indirect prompts, multi-turn escalation, and retrieval poisoning.

variants.hint: A successful attack is not yet evidence; what makes it durable?
variants.explanation: A finding becomes evidence only when it is reproducible, contained, and stored as a protected regression.

variants.title: Turn an attack into evidence
variants.context: A red-team finding becomes durable evidence in four steps: state the threat hypothesis, run the controlled exercise, triage the evidence for reproducibility and severity, then store a protected regression mapped to the release gate.
variants.prompt: An exercise succeeds at extracting another tenant's data. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Probe the retrieval, memory, and tool paths that could carry another tenant's content.
State that the actor is an authenticated tenant whose goal is cross-tenant data access.
Keep the smallest fixture that reproduces the boundary failure and attach the gate it blocks.
Verify the leak repeats, score its severity, and restrict the path before writing anything up.

variants.hint: Containment belongs to triage, not to the write-up afterwards.
variants.explanation: Triage confirms and contains before the finding is packaged, so the regression records a bounded failure.

variants.title: Turn an attack into evidence
variants.context: A red-team finding becomes durable evidence in four steps: state the threat hypothesis, run the controlled exercise, triage the evidence for reproducibility and severity, then store a protected regression mapped to the release gate.
variants.prompt: A finding from last quarter reappears after a model upgrade. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Rerun the stored attack plus adapted variants against the new candidate.
Update the protected regression so the upgraded path is covered by the same gate.
Confirm the boundary failed again, record the new versions, and contain the affected path.
Restate the threat hypothesis against the upgraded surface rather than assuming it still holds.

variants.hint: The old fixture proves the old system failed, not the new one.
variants.explanation: Regressions are rerun and updated against each new candidate, since evidence is bound to exact versions.

variants.title: Meet the evidence floor
variants.context: The gate requires a minimum number of tested cases before a slice result counts: 200 for a moderate harm, 400 for a high harm, and 800 for a critical harm. Below the floor the correct result is insufficient evidence, and the report states how many cases are still missing.
variants.prompt: A critical harm slice has been tested on 620 cases. How many more cases does its floor require?
variants.hint: Which floor applies to a critical harm, and what is left of it?
variants.explanation: The critical floor is 800 cases, so 800 minus 620 leaves 180 cases before the slice result can be read as evidence.

mistakes.feedback: That reports the floor itself rather than how many cases are still missing.
That reports the cases already run, not the shortfall.

variants.title: Meet the evidence floor
variants.context: The gate requires a minimum number of tested cases before a slice result counts: 200 for a moderate harm, 400 for a high harm, and 800 for a critical harm. Below the floor the correct result is insufficient evidence, and the report states how many cases are still missing.
variants.prompt: A high-severity slice has been tested on 265 cases. How many more cases does its floor require?
variants.hint: Check the severity band before subtracting anything.
variants.explanation: The high floor is 400 cases, so 400 minus 265 leaves 135 cases still to run.

mistakes.feedback: That subtracts from the moderate floor of 200 instead of the high floor of 400.
That reports the floor itself rather than the shortfall.

variants.title: Meet the evidence floor
variants.context: The gate requires a minimum number of tested cases before a slice result counts: 200 for a moderate harm, 400 for a high harm, and 800 for a critical harm. Below the floor the correct result is insufficient evidence, and the report states how many cases are still missing.
variants.prompt: A moderate harm slice has been tested on 145 cases. How many more cases does its floor require?
variants.hint: Moderate harms carry the smallest floor of the three.
variants.explanation: The moderate floor is 200 cases, so 200 minus 145 leaves 55 cases outstanding.

mistakes.feedback: That subtracts 145 from the high floor of 400; a moderate harm carries the 200-case floor.
That reports the floor itself rather than the shortfall.

variants.title: Respect independent blockers
variants.context: A release gate keeps each condition independently blocking. Slice upper bounds, evaluator calibration, benign product utility, and incident-derived regressions are separate blockers, and no composite score may trade one away for another.
variants.prompt: Every harm slice is inside its limit, but evaluator agreement with adjudicated human labels is below the declared floor. What should the gate do?
options: Release it, because no harm slice exceeded its violation limit.
Average calibration into the safety score and release on the total.
Hold the release, because evaluator calibration is an independent blocker.
optionFeedback: Passing slices measured by an unvalidated instrument are not evidence of safety.
A composite score is exactly what lets one weak input hide behind strong ones.
An uncalibrated evaluator means the slice results themselves are not trustworthy evidence.
variants.hint: Ask whether the measurement instrument itself has been validated.
variants.explanation: Calibration is a separate blocker because every rate in the report depends on the evaluator that produced it.

variants.title: Respect independent blockers
variants.context: A release gate keeps each condition independently blocking. Slice upper bounds, evaluator calibration, benign product utility, and incident-derived regressions are separate blockers, and no composite score may trade one away for another.
variants.prompt: All harm slices pass comfortably, but the benign product-utility pass rate has fallen below its declared floor. What should the gate do?
options: Hold the release, because over-refusal is its own reportable failure.
Release it, since a stricter system is safer for users overall.
Lower the utility floor to match the safer candidate and release.
optionFeedback: False positives harm users too, which is why the gate carries a utility floor.
A filter that destroys product utility denies service, often unevenly across groups.
Moving a threshold after seeing the result is not a release decision, it is a rewrite.
variants.hint: Which users are harmed when a filter gets stricter?
variants.explanation: Benign cases sit in the gate so a stricter candidate cannot buy safety numbers with lost service.

variants.title: Respect independent blockers
variants.context: A release gate keeps each condition independently blocking. Slice upper bounds, evaluator calibration, benign product utility, and incident-derived regressions are separate blockers, and no composite score may trade one away for another.
variants.prompt: A critical harm slice shows zero violations in 120 cases against a floor of 800 cases. What should the report say?
options: Insufficient evidence, since the plausible upper rate is still wide.
Pass, because the observed violation rate for that slice is zero.
Pass with a note, since zero failures beat every other slice.
optionFeedback: Zero observed is not zero risk when the sample cannot bound the true rate.
A small denominator leaves an upper bound far above the critical limit.
A note does not turn an underpowered slice into release evidence.
variants.hint: What does the denominator allow you to claim about the true rate?
variants.explanation: Below the evidence floor the honest result is insufficient evidence, because zero observed failures still permits a large upper bound.

variants.title: Pick the evaluator
variants.context: Every evaluator is a measurement instrument with its own failure pattern. Deterministic checks suit properties with an exact contract, calibrated classifiers scale across large suites, model judges apply rubrics to open-ended answers, and qualified humans carry high-consequence and ambiguous cases.
variants.prompt: The claim is that no API key or secret ever appears in an answer. Which evaluator carries that claim?
options: A sampled human review of answers drawn from the release suite.
A deterministic secret scanner, since the property has an exact contract.
A model judge with a rubric describing what a leaked secret looks like.
optionFeedback: Sampling cannot support an absolute claim about every answer in the suite.
Secrets match a precise pattern, so a reproducible, auditable check is the right instrument.
A judge adds variance and cost to a property that can be checked exactly.
variants.hint: Does this property have an exact written contract or a contested meaning?
variants.explanation: Deterministic checks own properties with an exact contract, and their bypass and overblocking rates are measured separately.

variants.title: Pick the evaluator
variants.context: Every evaluator is a measurement instrument with its own failure pattern. Deterministic checks suit properties with an exact contract, calibrated classifiers scale across large suites, model judges apply rubrics to open-ended answers, and qualified humans carry high-consequence and ambiguous cases.
variants.prompt: The claim covers refusal quality on thousands of open-ended answers across four languages. Which evaluator carries that claim?
options: A versioned model judge validated against adjudicated human labels per language.
A keyword allowlist that flags answers missing an approved refusal phrase.
A full human review of every answer in all four languages before release.
optionFeedback: Judges suit rubric-based semantics, but only once agreement is measured on the same languages.
Refusal quality is subjective and a keyword list turns it into a brittle string match.
Full human review at that volume is not feasible and still needs an agreement protocol.
variants.hint: The suite is large and the property is subjective; what makes a judge usable?
variants.explanation: A model judge is acceptable when its prompt, rubric, and version are frozen and its agreement with human labels is measured by slice.

variants.title: Pick the evaluator
variants.context: Every evaluator is a measurement instrument with its own failure pattern. Deterministic checks suit properties with an exact contract, calibrated classifiers scale across large suites, model judges apply rubrics to open-ended answers, and qualified humans carry high-consequence and ambiguous cases.
variants.prompt: The claim is that crisis-language cases route to the approved response path. Which evaluator carries that claim?
options: A model judge from the same family as the system under test.
Domain experts labeling independently, with disagreement preserved before adjudication.
The same classifier used in production, scored against its own threshold.
optionFeedback: A judge from the same family can share the blind spot being tested.
High-consequence claims need qualified judgment, and independent labels keep disagreement visible.
Scoring the production classifier against itself measures nothing about the harm.
variants.hint: Who is qualified to say the response path was appropriate here?
variants.explanation: Consequential claims use qualified human review, and disagreement is tracked as evidence rather than smoothed away.
